description: CS sophomore experienced in web and game development, leveraging AI for code assistance. Eager to do explore space data and build a accessible, engaging software that makes science fun to interact with
summary: Mars Valley is a 2D top-down survival game set on Mars. Stranded after a crash, the player gathers regolith, basalt, hematite, silica and water ice, crafts tools and components, builds pressurized domes with farms and power systems, survives dust storms, and repairs five ship modules to lift off. The world is not arbitrary: its biome grid is derived from real NASA Planetary Data System products for Gale Crater — MOLA elevation, TES thermal inertia and Odyssey GRS water-ice concentration — and its climate is calibrated against the NASA GSFC Mars climate model, so terrain, temperature, sunlight and ice availability reflect actual Martian conditions. The project turns planetary-science data into an engaging, understandable experience: instead of reading tables, players feel how scarce water is, how dust storms cut solar power, and how a habitat must be engineered. It is important because it makes Mars habitability and in-situ resource utilization tangible for students and the public. All data is public domain and credited in-game.
details:
Mars Valley is a single-player, top-down 2D survival and base-building game. After a crash landing, the player explores a procedurally classified Martian landscape, mines regolith, basalt, hematite, silica and subsurface water ice, refines them components, and crafts tools, life-support consumables and five ship parts. Progression follows a clear loop: better tools unlock new resources, which unlock better structures. The player builds pressurized domes with 12 interior slots and equips them with hydroponic farms, solar panels, batteries and bunks, managing energy and oxygen while dust storms reduce light and drop temperature. A mission chain (mine ice, plant and harvest potatoes, repair all five modules) culminates in repairing the ascent engine and lifting off.

What makes it grounded is that the map is not arbitrary. The 96×56 biome grid of Gale Crater is generated from NASA PDS data — MOLA topography, TES thermal inertia and Odyssey GRS water-ice abundance — and climate (temperature swings, solar input, dust optical depth) is calibrated against the NASA GSFC Mars climate model. Each biome therefore has plausible temperature, sunlight and ice fractions; gameplay values are simplified but derived rather than invented.

Benefits and impact: the game makes planetary science and in-situ resource utilization intuitive. Players learn why water ice is strategic, why dust storms threaten solar power, and why a habitat needs energy storage and life support — through play rather than a textbook. It targets students, educators and space enthusiasts and runs offline.

Tools: Godot 4.7.2 (Mono), C#, .NET 8, an engine-agnostic domain layer with xUnit tests, a Python data pipeline (download.py/generate.py) for the NASA products, procedural rendering via Godot's 2D draw API, and JSON saves. Creative choices include a strict domain/engine separation, data-driven catalogs for items/recipes/biomes, and a hand-built HUD. We weighed scientific accuracy against playability — keeping mechanics plausible while simplifying exact chemistry — and prioritized offline play, save/resume and rebindable controls.
